opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think people tend to blur those two things together, and they're really different properties of the system.

When we talk about how long you can play, we mean how long the model can keep generating a coherent, interactive world in real time as you move around and take actions. That's mostly about stability: does the visual quality hold up, does the world keep making sense frame after frame, does it avoid drifting into something weird. And you can keep going for a few minutes in a way that feels pretty continuous.

Memory is a different question. It's about whether the model remembers what it already showed you. If you paint something on a wall, walk away, and come back, is it still there, looking the same? That kind of consistency holds over a shorter horizon, roughly on the order of a minute. Beyond that, things you haven't looked at in a while can start to change.

So the distinction matters because it tells you what the system is actually good for. If you only quoted the play duration, people might assume the world is fully persistent for that whole time, and it isn't quite. If you only quoted the memory window, you'd undersell how long you can actually explore and interact. They're separate axes, and they also point to separate research problems. Extending stable generation is one challenge. Extending long-range memory, so the world stays consistent with everything that's happened, is another, and arguably a harder one. Being precise about both helps set the right expectations and makes it clearer where the next improvements need to come from.

r001.rationale: The response says Genie 3 can support a few minutes of continuous play while consistency holds for roughly a minute, so playable duration can exceed its memory span.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and it's one of those things that gets conflated a lot when people talk about the model. So with Genie 3 we say you can interact with the world for several minutes, and at the same time we say the model has roughly a minute of memory, and people hear those two numbers and think there's a contradiction, or that one of them is wrong. And they're really measuring two different things.

Play duration is about consistency. It's how long you can keep generating frames before the world starts to drift, before things stop looking coherent, before you get the kind of accumulated error that you see with autoregressive models where small mistakes compound and eventually the scene falls apart. Genie 3 stays visually and physically coherent for several minutes, and that's a big step from Genie 2, where you were talking about ten, twenty seconds before things degraded.

Memory is a different question. Memory is about what happens when you turn around. If you look at a wall, paint something on it, walk away, and come back thirty seconds or a minute later, is the painting still there? That's the model remembering what it generated earlier and conditioning on it, and that horizon is on the order of a minute. Beyond that, the model is still producing a perfectly plausible world, it just may not be the same world in the details you left behind.

And the reason I think it matters to keep them separate is that they fail differently and they're improved differently. You can have a model that generates coherent, stable video for a very long time but has no persistent memory at all, and that's fine for some use cases and useless for others. If you're an agent training in that environment and you need to go explore, come back, and act on something you saw earlier, memory is the thing you care about, not how long the stream stays pretty. If you're just experiencing the world, duration is what you notice. So when we talk about what Genie 3 can and can't do, especially for agent research, I want people to understand which of those two axes they're actually bumping into.

r001.rationale: The response says Genie 3 can remain coherent for several minutes while its memory horizon is about a minute, so playable duration exceeds memory.

astra-6.text: Because they’re measuring two different things. Play duration is how long you can keep interacting with the world, while memory is how far back the model can draw on what you’ve seen and done to keep that world consistent. You can continue playing even when some earlier events are outside that memory window. So a longer session doesn’t necessarily mean the model remembers everything from the beginning. The distinction matters especially when you revisit a place: continuing to generate the world and remembering exactly what you left there are different capabilities.

r001.rationale: It says play can continue even when earlier events fall outside the memory window, so playable duration can exceed memory span.
